A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that the AtEPSPS-T102I, P107A variant was not a very good target for glyphosate resistance in A. thalianae.
a 100‐fold increase in EPSPS resistance (AtEPSPS‐K i ∼ 50 μM) would only confer 4.3 to 16‐ fold resistance to glyphosate.
a 300‐fold increase in glyphosate resistance in a plant with the EPSPS‐TIPS mutation would require a 300‐ or more fold increase in the EPSPS gene copy number to achieve the same level of resistance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the EPSPS target site mutations that confer resistance to glyphosate have evolved in weeds and are likely to evolve in other species.
resistance is more difficult to evolve in a crop plant than in a weed, and that resistance is much easier to evolve in a weed that is not yet resistant to glyphosate.
it is possible for weeds to evolve a more potent EPSPS mutation than the TIPS mutation, which is the most potent EPSPS mutant that is known to occur in weeds.
